highlights: Gas diplomacy remains a strategic asset
State control over hydrocarbons holds firm

frictionVectors.title: European energy leverage
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains dependent on Algerian pipeline gas while pressing Algiers to expand supply and moderate pricing. This creates bargaining power but also exposes Algeria to external market and regulatory pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya threatens Algeria's border security and complicates its non-interventionist regional posture.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt exposure, especially to Chinese lenders, continues to constrain Luanda's autonomy over oil revenues and major infrastructure decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: US and European backing for the corridor increases Angola's geopolitical leverage over critical-mineral transport, while also inviting competition with Chinese commercial interests.

frictionVectors.title: Niger pipeline dependence
frictionVectors.details: The oil-export corridor linking Niger to Benin has become vulnerable to political tension and border restrictions, leaving Benin exposed to decisions made by neighbors and foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea security
frictionVectors.details: Benin relies on foreign naval, financial, and technical support to protect maritime trade and port infrastructure from piracy and wider regional insecurity.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is pressing for greater local value capture and marketing control, but remains exposed to the commercial and technological capabilities of international diamond firms.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-mineral infrastructure gap
frictionVectors.details: New copper, nickel, and energy projects could diversify the economy, yet rail, power, and water constraints increase reliance on foreign capital and regional transport networks.

highlights: Russian security ties replace Western influence

frictionVectors.title: Opaque gold-sector control
frictionVectors.details: Efforts to increase state control over gold production are undermined by informal mining, armed-group taxation, and limited regulatory capacity, allowing opaque external and illicit networks to capture value.

frictionVectors.title: Security dependency shift
frictionVectors.details: The junta's pivot away from Western partners toward Russian-linked security assistance increases military dependence on a new external actor without resolving the underlying territorial insecurity.

frictionVectors.title: RWANDA-BURUNDI SECURITY RIFT
frictionVectors.details: Mutual accusations over rebel support and border insecurity continue to restrict trade and regional cooperation. The dispute also increases Burundi's reliance on alternative diplomatic and security partners.

frictionVectors.title: MINERAL GOVERNANCE AND EXTERNAL FINANCE
frictionVectors.details: Gold and critical-mineral activity remains vulnerable to informal cross-border networks and opaque licensing. Chinese and Gulf-linked commercial interests compete with donor pressure for stronger oversight.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND MARITIME COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: The government is balancing European, North American, and Chinese interest in ports, logistics, and maritime surveillance. Dependence on external capital creates pressure over concession terms and strategic access.

frictionVectors.title: FISHERIES AND OCEAN RESOURCE CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and limited monitoring capacity challenge Cabo Verde's control over its exclusive economic zone. Climate stress and fuel costs further weaken domestic leverage over maritime resources.

highlights: Oil, gas, and timber remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: ANGLOPHONE CONFLICT
frictionVectors.details: Insurgency in the Northwest and Southwest continues to disrupt roads, agriculture, and public administration. The conflict limits Yaounde's effective control over local economic assets and encourages informal extraction.

frictionVectors.title: CHINESE INFRASTRUCTURE LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction remain important for roads, ports, and energy projects, but debt exposure and contract opacity constrain sovereign bargaining power. External firms retain a strong position in timber, mining, and hydrocarbons.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY AND MINING NEXUS
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security personnel provide regime protection while maintaining influence around gold and diamond activity. This arrangement reduces immediate military vulnerability but limits transparency and state control over resource revenues.

frictionVectors.title: PERIPHERAL CONTROL AND LOGISTICS
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups and weak transport links leave large parts of the country outside effective government administration. Dependence on neighboring corridors and foreign security providers makes resource exports vulnerable to coercion and disruption.

highlights: Oil revenues underpin a centralized state
Sahel and Sudan shocks raise exposure

frictionVectors.title: OIL DEPENDENCE AND PIPELINE LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenues remain central to fiscal stability, leaving the government exposed to foreign operators, export infrastructure, and price volatility. Limited diversification weakens sovereign control over long-term resource planning.

frictionVectors.title: SUDAN BORDER AND EXTERNAL SECURITY SUPPORT
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in Sudan drives refugee flows, arms trafficking, and cross-border insecurity in eastern Chad. N'Djamena is balancing ties with Gulf actors, neighboring governments, and residual Western security interests while seeking greater autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte and maritime jurisdiction
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, sustaining a sovereignty dispute over maritime boundaries, migration, and access to surrounding fisheries.

frictionVectors.title: Dependence on foreign capital
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on remittances, Gulf support, and external development finance, limiting its leverage over infrastructure and strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Mining concessions and critical minerals
frictionVectors.details: Cobalt, copper, and other mineral projects remain heavily shaped by foreign firms and trading networks, while weak enforcement limits domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern conflict and mineral smuggling
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups, regional networks, and illicit exporters continue to challenge Kinshasa's authority over mineral-producing areas and transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign oil operators remain central to production and technical capacity, while petroleum dependence exposes national revenue and policy space to external market conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-finance exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed infrastructure and lending provide essential connectivity but can increase long-term dependence on external contractors, creditors, and commodity-linked repayment structures.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cote d'Ivoire is expanding domestic processing and regulation, but foreign traders, financiers, and downstream manufacturers still capture substantial value.

frictionVectors.title: Security and infrastructure partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Western, Gulf, and Chinese partners support transport and security infrastructure, creating leverage risks as Abidjan balances diversification with strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military presence
frictionVectors.details: Major foreign bases provide revenue and security but constrain Djibouti's freedom of maneuver and make its sovereignty sensitive to great-power rivalry.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: The economy depends heavily on logistics, port concessions, and external financing, particularly Chinese-linked infrastructure, creating vulnerabilities around debt and asset control.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Heavy debt-service obligations and IMF conditions increase Gulf and Western influence over state assets, exchange-rate policy, and strategic infrastructure. Asset sales provide liquidity but reduce direct sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Water Security
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains a core sovereignty and food-security concern. Egypt is pursuing diplomatic and regional pressure while avoiding escalation that could destabilize the wider Nile basin.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Decline
frictionVectors.details: Maturing oil and gas fields are shrinking fiscal space, increasing dependence on new offshore investment and opaque production-sharing arrangements. Foreign energy firms retain decisive control over technology, financing, and market access.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Finance
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other external lenders remain important to major infrastructure projects, creating repayment and bargaining risks as hydrocarbon revenues weaken. The government retains political control but has limited economic diversification leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Copper, zinc, and gold projects provide revenue but rely on foreign operators, capital, and export routes. State participation preserves leverage, while sanctions history and governance concerns restrict investment options.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline gives it strategic value amid regional conflict and maritime competition. External security interest can generate bargaining power but also exposes the country to pressure from Gulf states, Ethiopia, and other Red Sea actors.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Economic Dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Africa remains central to Eswatini's trade, electricity supply, transport corridors, and investment flows. This dependence limits independent bargaining power over infrastructure and essential imports.

frictionVectors.title: Sugar Market Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The sugar sector depends heavily on preferential regional and European market access, leaving rural revenue exposed to trade-policy changes. Foreign buyers and downstream processors capture substantial value beyond the farm gate.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Negotiation Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The GERD strengthens Ethiopia's energy and regional bargaining position but remains a persistent source of tension with Egypt and Sudan. Financing, transmission infrastructure, and export markets still require external partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Strategic Assets
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and economic reforms are increasing the role of international lenders and foreign investors in telecoms, logistics, and industrial infrastructure. Liberalization may improve capacity while narrowing direct state control over strategic sectors.

highlights: Military transition seeks tighter control over oil and mining
Infrastructure diplomacy balances France, China, and Gulf capital

frictionVectors.title: Contract renegotiation risk
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are pressing for greater national participation in oil, manganese, and infrastructure ventures. Renegotiations could unsettle established French and Chinese commercial interests.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail dependence
frictionVectors.details: Export corridors remain concentrated around foreign-backed ports, railways, and logistics operators. Control of these networks limits Libreville's practical leverage over resource flows.

highlights: Small-state sovereignty constrained by aid and trade dependence
Senegal remains the decisive security and infrastructure partner

frictionVectors.title: Senegalese corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on access through Senegal for regional commerce, transport, and security cooperation. This creates leverage for Dakar over Banjul's strategic and economic choices.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and coastal pressure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and weak maritime enforcement threaten fisheries, a key livelihood and food-security asset. External aid and licensing arrangements can dilute national control over marine resources.

highlights: Debt restructuring narrows room for resource-sovereignty policies
Gold, lithium, and bauxite draw competing foreign investors

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Ghana is seeking more local processing and state participation in lithium, bauxite, and gold value chains. Fiscal pressure, however, strengthens the negotiating position of foreign investors and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and ecological loss
frictionVectors.details: Illegal gold mining continues to damage water systems and weaken state oversight. Foreign-linked supply chains and politically connected domestic actors complicate enforcement.

highlights: Bauxite dominance funds the state but reinforces external dependence
Simandou development could transform regional infrastructure

frictionVectors.title: Simandou corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore project is tying Guinea to large Chinese and international mining consortia, railways, and ports. Control over export infrastructure and revenue terms remains a central sovereignty concern.

frictionVectors.title: Junta-led contract uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: The military government is using mining negotiations to demand more domestic value capture while restricting political space. Sudden regulatory shifts could deter investment without guaranteeing stronger national control.

highlights: Cashew dependence leaves the economy exposed to external price swings
Political fragility limits control over ports and border trade

frictionVectors.title: Cashew value-chain capture
frictionVectors.details: Most cashew is exported with limited domestic processing, leaving farmers and the state vulnerable to foreign buyers and fluctuating prices. Efforts to build local processing face financing and governance constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Port and narcotics vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Weak maritime and customs institutions expose the country to illicit trafficking and outside commercial influence around Bissau's port. Political instability makes sustained control of logistics infrastructure difficult.

highlights: Ports and power remain strategic assets

frictionVectors.title: External debt and infrastructure finance
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service demands and IMF-linked reforms constrain Nairobi's room to direct public investment. Chinese, Gulf, and Western lenders remain influential in transport and energy decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Mombasa logistics competition
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is defending Mombasa's role as a regional gateway against competing corridors through Tanzania and Djibouti. Port concessions, logistics costs, and security in the wider western Indian Ocean remain sensitive sovereignty issues.

highlights: Dependence on South Africa remains acute

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Project dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's hydropower and water exports are economically vital but structurally tied to South African infrastructure, payments, and demand. Delays and financing for later project phases could weaken Maseru's bargaining position.

frictionVectors.title: Political and fiscal fragility
frictionVectors.details: Coalition instability and limited domestic revenue reduce the state's capacity to manage strategic water and infrastructure assets independently. South Africa remains the decisive external political and economic actor.

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore concession dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore operations and rail-port infrastructure provide revenue and jobs but leave Liberia dependent on foreign operators and commodity cycles. Contract transparency, local employment, and fiscal capture remain central sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor leverage
frictionVectors.details: Control of mining corridors and export terminals gives external firms significant influence over national logistics. Monrovia is seeking stronger domestic value capture while balancing investor confidence and infrastructure needs.

highlights: Oil remains divided by political authority

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented control of oil assets
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks continue to use production, export terminals, and budget access as leverage. International companies and foreign governments remain exposed to shutdowns, blockades, and competing claims over the National Oil Corporation.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military and energy competition
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia, Gulf states, and European actors pursue overlapping security and energy interests in Libya. Their involvement limits unified Libyan control over ports, bases, reconstruction, and offshore opportunities.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel and cobalt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led mining operations provide export earnings but expose Madagascar to volatile prices, imported inputs, and disputes over taxation and environmental costs. The state remains challenged in converting mineral wealth into broad domestic industrial capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-energy and port constraints
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable power, transport bottlenecks, and dependence on dedicated export infrastructure increase the leverage of international operators. Strategic mineral projects can therefore shape national energy and infrastructure policy more than domestic planning does.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF-backed reforms and bilateral debt restructuring are stabilizing the state, but creditor conditions still constrain policy autonomy and public investment.

frictionVectors.title: Mining infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign interest in uranium, rare earths, and other minerals is increasing, while weak transport and power networks limit Malawi's ability to capture downstream value.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is seeking greater state participation and revenue from industrial gold operations, creating sustained friction with foreign mining companies and investors.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cooperation with Russia's Africa Corps provides regime protection but increases external leverage over security policy, logistics, and potentially strategic-resource access.

frictionVectors.title: GTA gas project exposure
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal offers major fiscal and diplomatic gains, but shared infrastructure and revenue management create continuing bilateral and investor risks.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of extractives
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, gold, and emerging energy projects remain heavily dependent on foreign capital and technical expertise, limiting domestic value capture despite stronger state bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos transition risks
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago strengthens its diplomatic position, but the future of the Diego Garcia base and related security arrangements remains sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: External capital concentration
frictionVectors.details: The economy depends on foreign investment, tourism, and offshore financial activity, leaving it exposed to regulatory pressure from larger markets and shifts in global capital.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Phosphates, fisheries, ports, and renewable projects in Western Sahara remain central to Morocco's sovereignty strategy and a recurring source of tension with Algeria and external partners.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is leveraging ports, renewables, fertilizers, and automotive supply chains to reduce dependence on any single partner, while balancing EU, US, Gulf, and Chinese interests.

highlights: LNG ambitions constrained by Cabo Delgado insecurity
Port and gas corridors attract competing foreign capital

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado security and LNG restart
frictionVectors.details: Insurgency continues to raise costs and sovereignty concerns around offshore gas development. External military and private-security support remains important to protecting project corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Nacala and Beira corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Regional dependence on Mozambican ports creates leverage for South African, Chinese, Gulf, and Western investors. Maputo retains formal control, but financing and logistics contracts limit policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore oil ownership and licensing
frictionVectors.details: Major discoveries have increased bargaining power but also intensified scrutiny of foreign operators, fiscal terms, and environmental safeguards. Namibia is seeking greater domestic participation without deterring capital.

frictionVectors.title: Green-hydrogen infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large projects depend on foreign technology, export buyers, and concessional finance. Grid, water, and port investments could strengthen sovereignty if local procurement and skills transfer are enforced.

highlights: Junta tightens control over uranium and oil assets
Western rupture deepens Russian and regional alignment

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and mining concessions
frictionVectors.details: Relations with France and other Western operators have deteriorated as authorities seek revised terms and greater state control. Production and investment remain exposed to sanctions, political risk, and security disruptions.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and export-route vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The oil export route through Benin remains strategically sensitive amid diplomatic tensions and regional insecurity. Niger is pursuing diversified partnerships, including Russian support, but lacks equivalent infrastructure and financing capacity.

highlights: Oil-sector reform meets persistent production leakage
Dangote and gas projects expand domestic processing

frictionVectors.title: Foreign capital and oil-sector control
frictionVectors.details: Regulatory reforms and asset sales are intended to attract investment while increasing national participation. Production theft, pipeline sabotage, and opaque contracting continue to weaken effective resource sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Gas-to-power infrastructure bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Nigeria has substantial gas reserves but unreliable transmission, payment arrears, and security risks constrain domestic use. Foreign lenders and operators remain central to expanding pipelines, LNG, and power capacity.

highlights: Regional security ties drive external pressure

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals traceability dispute
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda is promoting itself as a formal minerals-processing and trading hub, but allegations that supply chains benefit from conflict-linked minerals from eastern DRC remain a major sovereignty and reputational risk.

frictionVectors.title: DRC conflict and diplomatic isolation
frictionVectors.details: Support for or alignment with M23 remains a central source of tension with Kinshasa, regional governments, and Western partners. Security partnerships and aid access increasingly carry political conditions that constrain Kigali's room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea Energy Competition
frictionVectors.details: Unproven offshore hydrocarbons attract foreign exploration interest, but São Tomé and Príncipe lacks the capital and technical capacity to control development terms independently.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port, electricity, and connectivity projects rely heavily on external partners, increasing exposure to competing Chinese, Portuguese, and regional interests.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater national control and transparency in mining and hydrocarbons, creating friction with multinational operators and prior concession arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Gas Monetization
frictionVectors.details: The GTA and Sangomar projects could strengthen fiscal sovereignty, but financing, local-content demands, and cross-border management with Mauritania remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Maritime Assets
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles must balance Indian, Chinese, Western, and Gulf interest in ports, surveillance, and maritime logistics while protecting control over fisheries and its exclusive economic zone.

frictionVectors.title: Climate and Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Climate vulnerability and dependence on tourism and external finance constrain the country's ability to fund resilient infrastructure without accepting restrictive foreign capital.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Dominance
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, and bauxite operations remain central to exports, leaving fiscal stability and land-use decisions vulnerable to multinational investors and commodity-price swings.

frictionVectors.title: Freetown Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Port expansion and logistics investment attract external partners, but weak bargaining power and limited oversight raise concerns about long-term concessions and strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Licensing and Maritime Claims
frictionVectors.details: Offshore petroleum ambitions are entangled with federal-regional disputes, foreign operators, and unresolved maritime governance, limiting credible national control over future revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Port Access Rivalries
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Ethiopia, and other actors compete for military, commercial, and corridor access, often reinforcing Somalia's fragmented security and infrastructure environment.

frictionVectors.title: Power-sector dependency
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability and grid constraints continue to limit industrial sovereignty. Fiscal pressure and dependence on external finance complicate Eskom reform and new generation investment.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral-investment bargaining
frictionVectors.details: South Africa seeks greater domestic value addition in platinum-group metals, manganese, and other strategic minerals while balancing Western, Chinese, and Gulf investment.

highlights: Oil lifeline exposed to Sudan war

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan relies on export infrastructure crossing Sudan, leaving oil revenues vulnerable to conflict, sabotage, and political leverage outside its territory.

frictionVectors.title: Resource-security competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign oil operators, neighboring states, and armed networks retain substantial influence over production and transit. Weak institutions limit the government's ability to convert resource income into sovereign development.

highlights: Gold and ports attract rival patrons

frictionVectors.title: Gold-war economy
frictionVectors.details: Competing military and commercial networks use gold production and trade to finance operations, drawing in regional intermediaries and external buyers.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea infrastructure contest
frictionVectors.details: Port access, transport corridors, and maritime influence are strategic assets for outside powers as the conflict fragments national control over infrastructure and trade.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Dar es Salaam-linked rail and port projects deepen ties with China, Gulf states, and other partners, creating financing opportunities alongside long-term dependency risks.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and gas control
frictionVectors.details: The government is pressing for greater domestic participation and revenue capture in mining and natural gas while seeking stable foreign capital for large projects.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional trade hinge

frictionVectors.title: Port-sector external influence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé and associated logistics networks attract foreign operators and capital, strengthening trade capacity while exposing strategic infrastructure to external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel spillover pressure
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and instability moving south from the Sahel raise security costs and may increase reliance on foreign intelligence, equipment, and border-support partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: EU Conditionality
frictionVectors.details: European financial support and migration cooperation give the EU substantial leverage over Tunisian policy. Fiscal pressure limits Tunis's bargaining power and policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains exposed to imported energy and external financing while domestic production and phosphate exports face structural constraints.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Contestation
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline strengthens Kampala's export prospects but faces sustained environmental, legal, and European political opposition. The project also deepens dependence on foreign capital and transit infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other external lenders remain important to Uganda's transport and energy buildout. Debt-service demands could constrain how much future resource revenue remains under national control.

frictionVectors.title: Copper Ownership Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is seeking greater domestic value addition and fiscal returns from copper while relying heavily on multinational capital and foreign technical expertise. Disputes over taxation, royalties, and processing capacity remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Power Supply Constraint
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower shortages threaten mines, manufacturing, and export earnings, increasing reliance on regional electricity imports and emergency investment. Climate variability makes the infrastructure vulnerability more persistent.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and Platinum Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is using export controls and beneficiation demands to capture more value from lithium, platinum, and other minerals, but Chinese and other foreign investors retain significant operational leverage. Limited capital and sanctions-related constraints weaken Harare's negotiating position.

frictionVectors.title: Monetary Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Persistent currency instability and limited reserves restrict the state's ability to manage resource revenues independently. Reliance on foreign currencies and external commodity finance amplifies outside influence over the economy.
